questions.stem: A doctor says an illness is caused by a pathogen. What does this term mean?
options: A white blood cell that engulfs and digests bacteria
A harmless microbe that lives on the skin or in the gut
An organism or agent that causes disease in its host
A chemical made by the body that destroys foreign cells
questions.explanation: A pathogen is any disease-causing agent, such as a virus or bacterium. Harmless microbes that live on and in the body are called normal flora and can help protect against pathogens.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes an infectious disease from a non-infectious one?
options: It is caused by the body's own cells dividing out of control
It is caused by a pathogen that can pass from one host to another
It is caused by an inherited allele passed from parents to children
It is caused by a poor diet that lacks particular vitamins or minerals
questions.explanation: Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens that can be transmitted between hosts. Inherited, nutritional and cancer-related diseases cannot be caught from another person.

questions.stem: Which feature is found in bacteria but not in viruses?
options: Genetic material, either DNA or RNA
An outer coat made largely of protein
The ability to cause disease in humans
Ribosomes for making proteins
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotic cells with their own ribosomes, cytoplasm and cell membrane, so they can make proteins and reproduce by themselves. Viruses consist of nucleic acid in a protein coat and must use a host cell's ribosomes.

questions.stem: Why are viruses described as obligate intracellular parasites?
options: They must be swallowed in food before they can cause an infection
They reproduce by binary fission once they are inside the host cell
They can reproduce only by using the machinery inside a host cell
They live only in the fluid between cells and never enter the cells
questions.explanation: Viruses have no metabolism of their own. They must enter a host cell and use its ribosomes, enzymes and energy to make new virus particles. Binary fission is how bacteria reproduce.

questions.stem: Some bacteria cause disease mainly by releasing toxins. Which is an example?
options: Tetanus, in which a toxin causes severe muscle spasms
Influenza, in which a toxin destroys cells of the airways
Measles, in which a toxin produces the characteristic rash
Hepatitis B, in which a toxin is spread by mosquito bites
questions.explanation: Tetanus is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, whose toxin interferes with nerves controlling muscles, causing spasms. Influenza, measles and hepatitis B are viral diseases.

questions.stem: What is a vector in disease transmission?
options: An organism, e.g. a mosquito, carrying a pathogen between hosts
A contaminated object, such as a doorknob, that holds a pathogen
A person who has recovered from a disease and is now immune to it
A drug that carries a vaccine into the cells of the immune system
questions.explanation: A vector is a living organism, often an insect, that transmits a pathogen from one host to another. Contaminated objects such as doorknobs are fomites, involved in indirect contact transmission.

questions.stem: Ross River virus is common in many parts of Australia. How is it transmitted to humans?
options: By sharing towels with an infected person
By eating undercooked chicken or eggs
By the bite of infected mosquitoes
By drinking water contaminated with faeces
questions.explanation: Ross River virus is spread by mosquitoes, which act as vectors. Reducing mosquito breeding sites and avoiding bites are the main ways to prevent infection.

questions.stem: A child catches a gastrointestinal infection after touching a toy that an infected child had handled earlier. Which mode of transmission is this?
options: Vector-borne, through an insect carrying the pathogen
Transfer of body fluids, through blood entering a wound
Indirect contact, through a contaminated object
Direct contact, through touching the infected child
questions.explanation: When a pathogen is passed on through a contaminated object or surface, called a fomite, rather than by touching the infected person, the transmission is indirect contact. Handwashing and cleaning surfaces reduce it.

questions.stem: Which diseases are spread mainly by the transfer of body fluids such as blood?
options: Ross River and dengue fever
Tetanus and impetigo
HIV and hepatitis B
Cholera and typhoid
questions.explanation: HIV and hepatitis B viruses are spread by blood and sexual fluids, for example through shared needles or unprotected sex. Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated food and water, and dengue and Ross River through mosquitoes.

questions.stem: After a flood, a town's drinking water is contaminated with sewage, and many people develop severe watery diarrhoea. Which bacterial disease is a well-known example of this mode of transmission?
options: Tetanus
Hepatitis B
Whooping cough
Cholera
questions.explanation: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae and spreads through water or food contaminated with faeces. Treating drinking water and safe sewage disposal prevent it.

questions.stem: Health authorities want to reduce the spread of a disease transmitted by contaminated food. Which measure targets this mode of transmission most directly?
options: Cooking food thoroughly and washing hands before preparing food
Spraying insecticide around homes to reduce insect populations
Screening donated blood before it is used in transfusions
Wearing gloves whenever handling needles and other sharp objects
questions.explanation: Thorough cooking kills pathogens in food, and handwashing stops pathogens being transferred to food. Insecticide targets vector-borne disease, and blood screening and glove use target transmission through body fluids.

questions.stem: Dengue fever occurs in parts of northern Queensland but not in Perth, even though infected travellers arrive in both places. What best explains this?
options: Its mosquito vector is established in north Queensland, not Perth
The dengue virus cannot survive in the colder drinking water supply of Perth
People in Perth have all been vaccinated against dengue as young children
Dengue spreads only by direct contact, which is less common in Perth
questions.explanation: A vector-borne disease can spread only where its vector lives. The mosquito that transmits dengue is found in parts of north Queensland, so local transmission can occur there after an infected traveller is bitten.

questions.stem: Which features of the skin make it an effective barrier against pathogens?
options: A tough outer layer of dead keratinised cells, and acidic oily secretions
A thin moist layer of living cells, and a constant supply of white blood cells
Cilia that sweep microbes away, and mucus that traps them as they land
Hairs that filter the air, and enzymes that digest every microbe on contact
questions.explanation: The outer skin is made of tightly packed dead cells filled with keratin, which pathogens find hard to penetrate. Sebum and sweat make the surface acidic and contain substances that inhibit microbes. Cilia and mucus line the airways, not the skin.

questions.stem: Tears and saliva contain lysozyme. How does it protect the body?
options: It breaks down the cell walls of some bacteria
It traps microbes in a layer of sticky mucus
It neutralises viruses by binding to their DNA
It raises the body temperature to slow microbes
questions.explanation: Lysozyme is an enzyme that digests the cell walls of many bacteria, killing them. Tears also wash particles and microbes from the surface of the eye.

questions.stem: How do the cells lining the trachea and bronchi protect the lungs?
options: Mucus traps microbes, and cilia sweep the mucus up to the throat
Cilia digest microbes, and mucus carries the products down into the alveoli
Mucus kills every microbe on contact, so cilia are needed only for breathing
Cilia produce antibodies, and mucus delivers them into the blood capillaries
questions.explanation: Goblet cells secrete mucus that traps dust and microbes, and the beating cilia move the mucus upwards to be swallowed or coughed out. Swallowed microbes are then exposed to stomach acid.

questions.stem: How does the stomach help defend against pathogens swallowed in food?
options: Its hydrochloric acid creates a low pH that kills many microbes
Its lining produces antibodies that coat every microbe swallowed
Its muscles grind microbes into pieces too small to cause harm
Its alkaline juices dissolve the protein coats of all viruses
questions.explanation: Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, which gives the stomach a pH of about 2 and destroys many swallowed pathogens. Antibody production is part of the specific immune response.

questions.stem: Which feature protects the urinary tract from infection?
options: The kidneys filter microbes out of the blood and store them
Cilia in the urethra sweep microbes upwards into the bladder
The regular flow of urine flushes microbes out of the urethra
The bladder lining produces hydrochloric acid that kills microbes
questions.explanation: Urination washes microbes out of the urethra before they can multiply, and the acidity of urine also inhibits some microbes. In the vagina, an acidic environment produced by normal bacteria helps prevent infection.

questions.stem: How does the external ear help protect against infection?
options: The eardrum secretes acid that kills microbes in the canal
Earwax and hairs in the ear canal trap dust and microbes
Cilia in the ear canal beat to move microbes into the throat
Lysozyme-rich tears drain through the ear canal and wash it
questions.explanation: Earwax (cerumen) and fine hairs in the outer ear canal trap particles and microbes, and earwax has antimicrobial properties. The ear canal is not lined with cilia.

questions.stem: A patient takes a long course of a broad-spectrum antibiotic and then develops a fungal infection in the mouth. What best explains this?
options: The antibiotic made the fungus resistant, so it grew faster than before
The antibiotic killed normal bacteria that compete with the fungus
The antibiotic is a fungus itself, so it has spread into the mouth
The antibiotic stopped the production of lysozyme in the salivary glands
questions.explanation: Normal flora occupy space and use nutrients, which limits the growth of pathogens. Broad-spectrum antibiotics kill many of these harmless bacteria, allowing fungi such as Candida, which antibiotics do not affect, to overgrow.

questions.stem: Coughing, sneezing and vomiting are described as defences against pathogens. How do they work?
options: They raise body temperature so microbes grow more slowly
They release antibodies that attach to microbes in the air
They increase blood flow to the airways to attract phagocytes
They forcibly expel irritants and microbes from the body
questions.explanation: These reflexes physically remove material from the airways or digestive tract, taking microbes with it. They are non-specific, responding to any irritant rather than a particular pathogen.

questions.stem: What are the four classic signs of inflammation?
options: Redness, heat, swelling and pain
Redness, fever, rash and itching
Paleness, cold, swelling and pain
Heat, sweating, coughing and fatigue
questions.explanation: Inflammation produces redness and heat from increased blood flow, swelling from fluid leaking into the tissue, and pain as nerve endings are stimulated. Loss of function is sometimes added as a fifth sign.

questions.stem: Which chemical, released by damaged tissue and mast cells, causes the blood vessels in an injured area to dilate and become leaky?
options: Insulin
Lysozyme
Acetylcholine
Histamine
questions.explanation: Histamine dilates local blood vessels and increases capillary permeability, producing redness, heat and swelling. Lysozyme is an enzyme that attacks bacterial cell walls.

questions.stem: Why is increased capillary permeability useful during inflammation?
options: It lets plasma proteins and phagocytes move from the blood into the tissue
It lets the pathogen escape from the tissue into the blood to be filtered
It lets red blood cells leave the blood to carry oxygen to the bacteria
It lets heat escape from the tissue so that the pathogen grows faster
questions.explanation: Leaky capillaries allow fluid containing clotting and defensive proteins to reach the tissue, and allow phagocytes such as neutrophils to squeeze through the capillary walls to the infection.

questions.stem: What is pus, which sometimes collects at a site of infection?
options: Clotted red blood cells sealing off a damaged vessel
Mucus secreted by the skin to trap invading microbes
Dead phagocytes, dead bacteria, tissue debris and fluid
Antibodies that have been secreted by the plasma cells
questions.explanation: Pus forms when large numbers of phagocytes, mainly neutrophils, die after engulfing bacteria. It contains these dead cells along with bacteria, broken tissue and fluid.

questions.stem: What causes the body temperature to rise during a fever?
options: Pyrogens reset the hypothalamus to a higher temperature set point
Bacteria release heat as they multiply rapidly inside the tissues
The skin stops producing sweat because of damage to sweat glands
The thyroid gland is infected and releases far more thyroxine
questions.explanation: Chemicals called pyrogens, released by white blood cells or by some pathogens, act on the hypothalamus and raise its set point. The body then conserves and produces heat until the new set point is reached.

questions.stem: At the start of a fever, a person shivers and feels cold even though their temperature is rising. Why?
options: The pathogen has damaged their thermoreceptors, so the skin cannot sense heat
Their blood is moving into the skin, which draws heat out of the body core
Their body is below the new, higher set point, so heat-gaining responses begin
Their body is above the new, lower set point, so heat-losing responses begin
questions.explanation: When pyrogens raise the set point, the body's actual temperature is suddenly below it, so the hypothalamus triggers shivering and vasoconstriction. When the fever breaks and the set point returns to normal, the person sweats and flushes to lose the extra heat.

questions.stem: Doctors often let a mild fever run its course. What benefit can a raised temperature bring during an infection?
options: It stops the body producing antibodies, saving energy for phagocytes
It stops the heart pumping blood to the area where pathogens are found
It slows some pathogens' reproduction and speeds immune reactions
It kills every pathogen in the body once the temperature passes 38 °C
questions.explanation: Many pathogens reproduce best at normal body temperature, so a higher temperature slows them, while chemical reactions in immune cells speed up. A fever does not kill all pathogens, and a very high fever can be dangerous.

questions.stem: Inflammation and fever are both described as non-specific responses. What does this mean?
options: They happen only when a pathogen has been met at least once before
They happen only in response to viruses and never to bacteria
They happen only after antibodies have been made to the pathogen
They happen in the same way whatever the type of pathogen involved
questions.explanation: Non-specific responses do not distinguish between particular pathogens and do not need prior exposure. Responses that depend on recognising a particular antigen and are faster on repeat exposure are specific.

questions.stem: Which white blood cells are the main phagocytes that arrive at a site of inflammation?
options: B lymphocytes, followed by plasma cells
T lymphocytes, followed by memory cells
Red blood cells, followed by platelets
Neutrophils, followed by macrophages
questions.explanation: Neutrophils usually arrive first in large numbers and engulf microbes. Monocytes follow and develop into macrophages, which engulf microbes and debris. Lymphocytes belong to the specific response.

questions.stem: A patient with a cold asks for antibiotics, and the doctor explains they will not help. What is the biological reason?
options: Viruses lack cell walls and bacterial ribosomes, which antibiotics target
Viruses are much larger than bacteria, so antibiotics cannot reach their genetic material
Viruses live only in the blood, where antibiotics are broken down before they act
Viruses reproduce so slowly that antibiotics are excreted before they take effect
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on features of bacterial cells, such as cell wall synthesis or bacterial ribosomes. Viruses have none of these and reproduce inside host cells using host machinery, so antibiotics have nothing to act on.

questions.stem: Penicillin kills bacteria but does not harm human cells. What explains this?
options: It blocks mitochondria, which bacteria have and human cells lack
It stops all protein synthesis, which human cells can do without
It stops bacteria building cell walls, which human cells do not have
It destroys DNA, which human cells protect inside a strong cell wall
questions.explanation: Penicillin interferes with the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall, causing bacteria to burst. Human cells have no cell wall, so they are unaffected. Bacteria lack mitochondria, so that option reverses the facts.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a broad-spectrum and a narrow-spectrum antibiotic?
options: A broad-spectrum antibiotic is taken by mouth; a narrow-spectrum one is injected into a vein
A broad-spectrum antibiotic acts on many types of bacteria; a narrow-spectrum one on a few
A broad-spectrum antibiotic acts on bacteria and viruses; a narrow-spectrum one on bacteria only
A broad-spectrum antibiotic is given in large doses; a narrow-spectrum one in small doses
questions.explanation: Spectrum refers to the range of bacteria affected. Narrow-spectrum drugs are preferred when the bacterium is known, because they disturb normal flora less and add less pressure for resistance. Neither type works on viruses.

questions.stem: How do most antiviral drugs work?
options: They block a particular stage of the virus's replication cycle
They break down the cell walls of the virus so that it bursts open
They stimulate the production of antibodies against every virus
They destroy all host cells that contain any type of virus particle
questions.explanation: Antivirals block specific steps, such as the virus entering cells, copying its genetic material or being released from the cell. Viruses have no cell walls, and destroying host cells would be harmful.

questions.stem: Why is it generally harder to develop antiviral drugs than antibiotics?
options: Viruses have thicker cell walls than bacteria, so drugs cannot get inside them
Viruses are always found outside cells, where drugs are quickly broken down
Viruses have no genetic material, so there is nothing for a drug to target
Viruses use the host cell's own machinery, so drugs risk harming host cells too
questions.explanation: Because viruses replicate inside host cells using the cell's ribosomes and enzymes, there are fewer virus-only targets. A useful antiviral must act on a viral feature without damaging the host cell, and is usually specific to one virus or a small group.

questions.stem: A drug for influenza blocks a viral enzyme that new virus particles need in order to be released from an infected cell. What would this drug achieve?
options: It would slow the spread of virus to new cells, but not cure cells already infected
It would destroy every infected cell, removing the virus from the body at once
It would prevent the virus entering any cells, so no cell could be infected again
It would make the person immune for life by producing memory B cells directly
questions.explanation: Blocking release traps new virus particles in the cell, limiting the spread to other cells and giving the immune system time to clear the infection. It does not destroy infected cells or create immunity, which requires the person's own immune response.

questions.stem: A doctor tells a patient to finish the whole course of antibiotics even after they feel better. How does this help reduce antibiotic resistance?
options: It allows the patient's immune system to produce more antibiotics
It ensures the virus causing the infection is fully destroyed too
It kills less susceptible bacteria that survive the first days
It gives the bacteria time to become used to the antibiotic slowly
questions.explanation: The most susceptible bacteria die first. Stopping early can leave behind the more resistant survivors, which multiply and may pass on resistance genes. Resistance arises by mutation and natural selection, not by bacteria getting used to a drug.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how antibiotic resistance spreads through a population of bacteria?
options: Resistant bacteria survive exposure, reproduce and pass on resistance genes
Bacteria develop resistance in response to the antibiotic, then pass it on
Human cells become resistant to the antibiotic and protect the bacteria
The antibiotic changes into a weaker form after it has been used repeatedly
questions.explanation: Some bacteria carry alleles for resistance that arose by chance mutation. The antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, so the resistant ones survive and multiply, and resistance genes can also pass between bacteria on plasmids. This is natural selection.
